title: Natural refineries and computing analogies
outcome: Compare an observed cleanup mechanism to a bounded computing analogy.
show: Sort the original examples into fungi, plants, microbes and animals. Put a computing analogy beside each group and name what would need to be measured.
concepts: Oyster mushrooms and Pestalotiopsis are the starting examples for studying substrate changes and filtering. Evidence for a specific compound and setting is needed before generalizing to another substance.

Sunflowers, spider plants, snake plants and water hyacinth prompt questions about uptake, indoor-air claims and cleanup scale. A contaminant transferred to biomass can still require controlled handling.
Ideonella sakaiensis is a documented PET example under study conditions. Geobacter and Alcanivorax borkumensis illustrate different research questions about electron transfer and oil degradation.
Oysters, clams and mussels illustrate filtration. Waxworms and mealworms prompt questions about plastic fragmentation, breakdown products and what the observations establish.
Record the compound, conditions, change, and remaining material. Elements such as heavy metals can move or change chemical form, and radioactive isotopes remain radioactive until they decay.
replicate: Make an input, output, and remaining-material diagram using paper tokens or a published study.
Relate one example to deduplication, quarantine, or monitoring. Identify the actual source of electricity and work in a Bitcoin mine.
check: What evidence distinguishes removal from transfer?
Measure the substance in both the original medium and the receiving material. Include any breakdown products and use appropriate controls.
sources: Russell et al. · Fungi and polyester polyurethane
Cummings and Waring · Indoor plants and air cleaning
Review · Electron transfer beyond the outer membrane
